meta.ogTitle: Who really said “I simply can't bear fools” / “Apparently, your mother could”?
meta.ogDescription: Not Cerf's line, and probably not Parker's: the jest ran in a Boston paper in 1858, decades before either of them told it.

answer.label: Not Bennett Cerf — a 19th-century joke he retold
answer.authorDates: First recorded 20 February 1858 · Ballou's Pictorial, Boston · credited to Dorothy Parker from 1941 · retold by Bennett Cerf in 1944
answer.sourceLine: Bennett Cerf printed this exchange in Try and Stop Me (Simon & Schuster, 1944) as a shipboard anecdote about Dorothy Parker — he was the anthologist, not the author, and he never claimed the line. The joke itself was already in print in Boston on 20 February 1858, thirty-five years before Parker was born, as “He can’t bear a natural fool” / “Unfortunately your mother could.” Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the jest was not formulated by Parker either.

source.excerpt: One pedant speaking of another says, “He can’t bear a natural fool;” whereupon the other replies, “Unfortunately your mother could.”
trail: 20 February 1858 — Boston. “He can’t bear a natural fool;” / “Unfortunately your mother could.” Printed as an unattributed filler in Ballou’s Pictorial Drawing-Room Companion; the sentence is present in the scanned issue at the Internet Archive ↗.

1867 and 1887 — San Francisco, then the wire. The Golden Era runs the trimmed version (“A pedant said to an old farmer that he could not bear a fool; he replied, ‘Your mother could.’”), and twenty years later the gag is recycled as a newspaper anecdote about young Maine editors — both dated and transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗.

June 1941 — the first Parker credit. A reader’s submission to The Reader’s Digest column “Party Chatter” puts the line in Parker’s mouth at a party; this is the earliest attribution to her that QI located ↗.
1944 — the version that stuck. Bennett Cerf moves the scene to a ship and adds the drunk in Try and Stop Me, published by Simon and Schuster ↗; from here the anecdote enters general circulation.
source.excerptNote: The earliest known printing of the joke, in a column of one-line fillers, immediately after a gag about a boy in an oversized hat and a flour-barrel rebus. The cast is two pedants; the famous wit, the drunk and the ocean liner arrive much later.

source.rightsNote: The 1858 Ballou’s Pictorial wording quoted above is long out of copyright and freely reproducible. The familiar modern phrasing is a different matter: its earliest documented appearances are The Reader’s Digest of June 1941 and Bennett Cerf’s Try and Stop Me of 1944, both first published well after 1930, so we treat that wording as in-copyright to those publications rather than claiming public domain for it.

author.name: Bennett Cerf
author.kicker: The man who put it in print
author.heading: About Bennett Cerf
author.metaLine: 1898–1971 · Random House co-founder, anecdote anthologist & What's My Line? panelist
author.bio: Bennett Cerf co-founded Random House and spent sixteen years grinning through the panel game show What’s My Line?, but his side career was collecting other people’s wisecracks. In 1944 he published Try and Stop Me, the first of a long run of joke-and-anecdote books, and it is there — page 112 — that the “bear fools” retort reaches a mass audience, told as something Dorothy Parker said to a drunk on a ship. Cerf was a superb curator and a careless custodian of provenance: his books are why dozens of unattached jokes now travel with famous names welded to them, and why his own name sometimes gets welded on in turn.

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This retort is one of the most widely travelled jokes in English, and almost every telling attaches a name to it. The names are all later than the joke.

items.why: Cerf’s Try and Stop Me (Simon & Schuster, 1944) is where most modern retellings ultimately come from, and a line quoted “from Bennett Cerf” is really a line quoted from a book Cerf compiled. He presents it as Dorothy Parker’s remark to a shipboard admirer — page 112, per Quote Investigator ↗, which verified the book in hardcopy. Cerf claimed no authorship of it.

The earliest cite crediting Parker that Quote Investigator ↗ located is a reader’s submission to the “Party Chatter” column of The Reader’s Digest in June 1941, contributed by one Olga Swanson. The joke had been in print since 1858 and Parker was born in 1893. She may well have used it — QI allows that — but using a joke is not writing one.

Cerf’s 1944 text has the longer “your mother did not have the same difficulty,” and quote sites still circulate that version sourcelessly — see this typical listing ↗, which gives Parker and no citation at all. The three-word core — “Your mother could” — goes back to the anonymous 1867 newspaper filler; the exact four-word form everyone quotes, “Apparently your mother could,” is first documented in The Reader’s Digest of June 1941, the same item that first credits Parker. Both texts per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: It is an anonymous American jest: printed in Boston in 1858, still working the papers in 1867 and 1887, credited to Parker from 1941 and popularised by Cerf in 1944. Per Quote Investigator ↗, neither of them formulated it.

context.heading: Why an anecdote book is not a source
lead: Anecdote collections were the viral feeds of their day, and Bennett Cerf ran the biggest one. Try and Stop Me sold enormously in 1944, and the deal it offered readers was that every gag came with a famous face attached — a nameless joke is just a joke, but a joke Dorothy Parker aimed at a drunk on a boat is a story. The attribution was the entertainment, which is exactly why it should not be treated as evidence.

The tell here is the punchline itself. The crisp form was already in print in June 1941 — “Apparently your mother could,” in the same Reader’s Digest squib that first put the line in Parker’s mouth — and it echoes the anonymous 1867 newspaper filler almost exactly. Cerf’s 1944 retelling is the one that padded it, to “your mother did not have the same difficulty,” and the padded version is what survives on sourceless quote sites. The sentence people actually quote is the magazine’s, not the bestseller’s.
detailsBody: 1858, Boston. A one-line filler in a “Joker’s Budget” column in Ballou’s Pictorial Drawing-Room Companion, printed immediately after a hat gag and a flour-barrel rebus and just before a bookstore gag, with two pedants as the cast.
1867, San Francisco. The same quip resurfaces on the opposite coast in The Golden Era, recast as a pedant and an old farmer, and with the punchline already trimmed to four words: “Your mother could.”

1887, Maine by way of New Jersey. Reworked as a newspaper anecdote titled “Wide-Awake Boy Editors,” in which young editors print an angry correspondent’s “I could never bear a fool” and append a single editorial line beneath it. Dates and texts for all three per Quote Investigator ↗.
context.pull: The joke did not need Dorothy Parker. Dorothy Parker’s legend needed jokes.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator dates the jest to Ballou's Pictorial (20 Feb 1858, “Joker's Budget,” p. 127), records 1867 Golden Era and 1887 “Wide-Awake Boy Editors” versions, names The Reader's Digest of June 1941 (“Party Chatter,” p. 49, contributed by Olga Swanson) as its earliest cite crediting Dorothy Parker, cites Bennett Cerf's Try and Stop Me (Simon & Schuster, 1944, p. 112) for the shipboard anecdote, and concludes neither jest in Cerf's anecdote was formulated by Parker.

The 20 February 1858 issue of Ballou's Pictorial Drawing-Room Companion (vol. 14, no. 8) contains the text: “One pedant speaking of another says, ‘He can't bear a natural fool;’ whereupon the other replies, ‘Unfortunately your mother could.’” — confirmed via the item's own full-text index.
Bennett Cerf's Try and Stop Me: A Collection of Anecdotes and Stories, Mostly Humorous was published by Simon and Schuster in 1944.

Bennett Cerf lived 25 May 1898 – 27 August 1971, co-founded Random House, appeared for 16 years on What's My Line?, and in 1944 published the first of his books of jokes and anecdotes, Try and Stop Me.
Dorothy Parker was born 22 August 1893 and died 7 June 1967; she was an American poet, critic and fiction writer and a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table.
Wikiquote's Dorothy Parker page contains no entry for “can't bear fools” or “your mother could” in any section, including Misattributed.
A typical quote-listing site circulates the exchange credited to Dorothy Parker with no source given, in the wording “Apparently your mother did not have the same difficulty.”
